name: Fixed lingual retainer
lead: A fixed lingual retainer is a thin wire bonded to the tongue-side surfaces of the front teeth, most often the lower front teeth, to hold them in position after orthodontic treatment. It helps people keep the straight, even smile they paid for: because the wire stays in place around the clock, the teeth have less opportunity to drift back toward their old crowded, rotated or gapped positions, and the visible result of braces or aligners is preserved. Because it sits behind the teeth, it is not visible from the front.[1]

After active treatment ends there is a lifelong tendency for teeth to relapse, which orthodontic texts attribute to recoil of the gum-attachment fibres, pressure from lips, cheeks and tongue, the bite, and continued growth and ageing changes.[1] Retainers are meant to hold the teeth long enough for the surrounding tissues to adapt. Fixed versions are typically bonded to the six front teeth or only the canines, and are used where relapse is considered more likely, such as after correction of severe rotations, gaps between the central incisors or in patients with periodontal disease.[1]

Because it is not removed, it needs little patient cooperation, but it is harder to clean around than removable retainers.[1] Published work has compared fixed and removable retainers on microbial levels and gum health, tested different wire materials from braided steel to fiber composite, titanium and 3D-printed resin, and examined bond failure.[3][4][7][10]

paras: The appliance is a short length of wire shaped to follow the inner surface of the lower (or sometimes upper) front teeth and bonded to each tooth with a small amount of dental composite after the tooth surface is etched. The composite usually covers the wire while leaving the spaces between teeth open for cleaning.[1] Two arrangements are described as most common: a multistrand wire bonded to all six anterior teeth, and a round stainless steel wire bonded to the canines only.[1] Wires may be smooth or flexible spiral (multistrand) types.[1]

A fixed retainer is sometimes combined with a removable retainer, for example a Hawley plate or vacuum-formed (clear plastic) retainer on the opposite arch.[1][3] The orthodontist sets how long it is worn; some advise wearing retainers for a fixed period and others indefinitely.[1]

Orthodontic texts describe relapse as the tendency of teeth to return toward their original positions after treatment. Contributing factors listed include elastic recoil of the periodontal fibres, pressure from the surrounding soft tissues, the occlusion, and continued growth and development.[1] Holding the teeth for a period lets those fibres and the supporting bone adapt, which can limit changes to the final tooth position.[1]

The lower front teeth are the area most often discussed in this context. A long-term study of 22 non-extraction cases, all without retainers for at least five years at follow-up, looked at stability after prolonged retention with a mandibular fixed lingual retainer, which averaged 8.4 years.[2] Reports of this kind are part of why fixed wires are often chosen for the lower front teeth.

Conventional versions use multistrand stainless steel wire bonded with composite. Alternatives studied include fiber-reinforced composite, CAD/CAM titanium retainers milled to a digital design, and 3D-printed nanoceramic resin retainers.[4][7][8] Laboratory work has also examined the mechanical behaviour of polyetheretherketone (PEEK) rods as a metal-free option, using finite-element modelling and bending tests.[13] Corrosion resistance of different fixed retention appliances has been compared in the laboratory.[9]

Reports on technique cover ways to hold the wire in position during bonding, including stabilising springs and resin-transfer bonding methods intended to shorten chair time.[14][15] Digitally designed retainers are promoted on the grounds that they reduce operator variability and chair time, which is the stated motivation of the titanium CAD/CAM trial.[7]

sections.h: Role in looking better after braces
paras: For people who have had braces or aligners to fix crowding, rotations or spacing in the front teeth, the lower front teeth are the area orthodontic texts single out as most prone to drifting back. Fixed retainers are described as the best-performing retainer type for holding the lower incisors, ahead of vacuum-formed and Hawley retainers.[1] The appearance payoff is therefore continuity: the alignment achieved at the end of treatment is the one still visible years later.[2]

The wire's position behind the teeth, and the fact that it requires no daily decision to wear it, are the features proponents emphasise compared with removable retainers, which depend on the wearer putting them in as advised.[1] Removable options have their own selling points: they are easier to clean, and clear vacuum-formed retainers are nearly invisible and interfere less with speech.[1] Hawley retainers are described as having less appealing aesthetics and more speech interference, and in one comparison wearers reported more embarrassment about them than about clear retainers.[1]

Wikipedia's overview lists Hawley, vacuum-formed, Begg and Barrer designs as removable types, which can be worn part-time or full-time as advised and are easier to clean than fixed wires.[1] Vacuum-formed retainers are usually worn overnight; if worn while eating they can hold food and sugars against the teeth.[1] People with bruxism may break them more quickly.[1]

A fixed wire does not depend on wear schedules, but it cannot be taken out for cleaning and needs more hygiene attention.[1] Orthodontists sometimes combine the two, using a fixed wire on the lower teeth and a removable appliance on the upper.[1][3] A randomized comparison of 45 patients assigned to fixed, vacuum-formed or Hawley retainers is the main head-to-head report on gum health and bacteria.[5]

Fixed retainers are described as the best-performing retainer type for holding the lower incisors.[1] A study of 22 non-extraction cases reported on long-term stability after prolonged retention with a mandibular fixed lingual retainer, averaging 8.4 years.[2] A trial compared the number of bite contacts over one year in patients given wraparound Hawley retainers or maxillary Jensen plates with mandibular fixed retainers.[3] Surgical release of gum fibers (fiberotomy) and its effect on one-year rotational relapse has also been studied.[6]
A 2024 commentary summarising a systematic review and network meta-analysis concluded that CAD/CAM fixed retainers may be as effective as conventional ones.[12]

Poorly cleaned retainers, fixed or removable, can lead to plaque, cavities and gum inflammation.[1] Fixed retainers need more attention from the patient than removable ones to prevent plaque build-up and gum inflammation around the wire.[1] A randomized comparison of 45 patients assigned to fixed, vacuum-formed or Hawley retainers examined salivary microbial levels and periodontal status.[5] A cross-sectional study asked patients up to ten years after treatment about oral hygiene, periodontal health and satisfaction with retention.[11]

Debonding is a recognised issue. Bond failure rate over 24 months has been examined in 86 young patients in relation to whether a self-etch primer was used on mandibular bonded retainers made from six-stranded steel wire.[10] Orthodontists typically advise periodic checks so that a loose or broken wire can be repaired, since an unnoticed debond lets teeth move.

Guidance summarised in the orthodontic literature is that a fixed retainer cannot be removed and is cleaned as part of the evening home-care routine, with a wet toothbrush and non-abrasive toothpaste, and attention to the plaque that gathers along the wire.[1]

Randomized trials have compared fiber-reinforced composite with multistrand steel wire in 60 patients for bleeding index and pocket depth over 12 months, titanium CAD/CAM with conventional 8-strand steel retainers bonded on the six lower front teeth (alignment stability and gum health over six months), and fixed versus removable retainers in 45 patients.[4][5][7]

Other studies include a long-term case series of 22 patients, a one-year bite-contact study of 60 subjects including a normal-occlusion control group, a cross-sectional patient-reported survey, and a fiberotomy relapse study.[2][3][6][11] A 2024 evidence-based dentistry commentary on a network meta-analysis of CAD/CAM versus conventional fixed retainers was published as well.[12] Laboratory studies cover 3D-printed resin, PEEK and corrosion behaviour.[8][9][13]

card.summary: A wire glued behind the lower front teeth to stop relapse; it stays put, but is harder to clean.
card.aka: Bonded retainer, permanent retainer, lingual wire
card.note: Hygiene around the wire matters; bonds can fail.

quick.overview:
A fixed lingual retainer is a small wire bonded behind the front teeth, usually the lower ones, to keep them from shifting after braces.

It works continuously without the patient having to remember to wear it, but cleaning around it is harder. Trials have compared materials and fixed versus removable designs.
quick.mechanism: The wire holds adjacent teeth together so they cannot drift back toward their old positions.
quick.risks: Plaque and gum inflammation if not cleaned well, and the bond can fail, which is why bonding techniques have been studied.

Alignment from braces or aligners stays visible
angle.text: A fixed retainer is used after braces or aligners to keep the front teeth where treatment put them. It is bonded behind the teeth, so the straight smile is maintained without a visible appliance and without the wearer having to remember to put anything in.
